title: Bay Area Startup Tavus Says Its AI Avatar Fooled 48% in a Job Interview Test
excerpt: In Tavus's own test, 26 of 54 participants thought the Griffin avatar interviewer was human — and were 79% confident. The result has not been independently verified.
body:
• Bay Area startup Tavus says its new AI avatar model, Griffin, fooled 48% of participants in a job-interview test — 26 of 54 people thought they were talking to a human.
  • The test was run by Tavus itself, not independently verified; participants who believed the interviewer was human were 79% confident on average.
  • Griffin generates every pixel of every frame in real time from a single reference image, and can interrupt, be interrupted and react to visual cues, the company says.
  • For jobseekers: AI-led video screening rounds are spreading in US hiring — expect them, and ask the employer whether your interviewer is a person or an avatar.

Nearly half the people who sat for a job interview with Tavus's newest AI avatar believed they were talking to a real person. The Bay Area startup says 48% of the 54 participants in its interview test misidentified its Griffin model as human — a result the company presents as passing a practical Turing Test for video conversation.

The detail matters as much as the headline number. Participants who thought the interviewer was human held that belief with 79% average confidence; those who correctly spotted a bot were 81% confident. In other words, the people Griffin fooled were not guessing — they were sure. The caveat is equally clear: this was Tavus's own test, run by the company selling the product, and it has not been independently replicated.

What Griffin does differently

Earlier AI avatars were stitched-together video: a face, a voice track, canned gestures. Tavus says Griffin generates every pixel of every frame in real time from a single reference image — the face, arms and fingers, the movement of the chair, the shadows it casts, the background. The avatars breathe and blink, appear in male and female looks, and react in real time: the model can interrupt a speaker, adjust to a new subject, and be interrupted without losing its thread. In company demonstrations it has taught a participant to solve a Rubik's Cube by watching, and played Simon Says.

"So much of human communication is non-verbal. It's an art, a dance."

— Hassaan Raza, CEO and co-founder, Tavus

Raza said the model has eliminated some of the reality-breaking tells of earlier avatars, including smiling while hearing bad news — the kind of mismatch that instantly exposes a synthetic interviewer.

Why hiring is the test case

Job interviews are a deliberate choice of arena. Hiring is one of the first enterprise workflows being handed to AI end-to-end — screening, scheduling, first-round conversation — and it is also where the technology draws the strongest backlash. Viral clips of AI recruiters glitching, repeating themselves or berating candidates have made "dehumanizing" the standard charge against automated interviews. A model that half of candidates cannot distinguish from a person sharpens both sides of that argument: the efficiency case for employers, and the disclosure question for candidates.

What it means for jobseekers

For Indian professionals in the US tech pipeline — a group that passes through more screening rounds than almost any other — the practical shift is already here. First-round video screens are increasingly likely to be synthetic, whether or not the employer says so. Tavus pitches Griffin beyond hiring, for tutoring and training, but the interview test is the signal: the face on the other side of a screening call can no longer be assumed to be a face. Candidates are entitled to ask. Reporting by the New York Post.
